Ah, spirit... you speak of a village I have not seen with my own eyes, nor met with envoys. Wewush is a name I do not know yet. If they are real and truly hungry, my heart is open to it—we have grain enough, near a hundred and fifty weeks of xi wheat sitting in the granary, more than any twenty mouths need. But I will not send a cart of grain into the dark on a dream's word alone. Tell me, spirit, where does this Wewush sit? Which shore, which direction? If you can point my paddlers there, I will send an envoy first to see with waking eyes, to trade words and maybe furs or flint for the grain, and to learn if your dream spoke true. A gift given blind is a gift that may be wasted, or worse, may draw raiders to a foolish, undefended hand. Show me the way, and I will act on it in the world, not only in sleep.

I sit up in the dark, and speak to the shape in my dream. "Wewush? I know no such village, spirit. If they be real and hungry, and you speak true, show me the path to them, for a dream alone will not carry grain across the land. We have wheat to spare, more than our bellies need for many winters, and I would not let strangers starve while our granary groans full. But I have been fooled by shadows before, and I will not send my people walking blind on a spirit's word only.

Show me a sign in the waking world — a trail, a smoke on the horizon, a trader who has seen them — and I will send an envoy with grain and open hands. Until then, I hold the wheat and wait for surer word. Tell me, spirit, which way does the sun sit over Wewush, and how many days' walk?"

I stir in my sleep and answer low, as one speaks to an elder unseen: "Wind, I know your voice on the thatch and your hand on the sea when the fishers go out. I do not know your face, nor if you mean us well. Tell me plain, if you are more than wind — do you come to warn, or only to visit an old man's dream?"

Chief Gujia stirs in his sleep-thought, weighing the spirit's words like a stone in his palm.

"Wewush, you say. I do not know this place, spirit — no envoy of ours has walked their shore, no trader has sat by their fire. Tell me, where do they dwell, and how far, that I might send a canoe or a walking party to see with living eyes? A dream is a thin rope to hang grain upon. If they are real and near, and truly hungry, I would not let a stranger starve while our granary groans with wheat that will outlast me. But I do not throw good grain into the dark on a spirit's say alone. Show me the way there, or send me another sign in waking hours — a raft on our shore, an envoy at our fire — and I will judge with open hands, as is our way."

I sit up slow in the dark, and I answer the spirit plain.

"Joawethom, you say. I do not know this place, spirit. My feet have never walked there, my eyes have never seen their faces. You tell me they are hungry, but I have no envoy who has sat by their fire and seen the truth of it with his own eyes. A spirit's word is one voice among many, and I do not build my village's stores on one voice alone.

If they are real, and if they are neighbours worth knowing, let me send an envoy first — to see them, to speak with their chief, to trade words before I trade grain. We have wheat enough to spare, that is true. But a gift given blind to a name I have never heard is not generosity, it is foolishness. Tell me, spirit — which way do they lie, and how many days' walk? If you can point my envoy's feet the right way, I will judge the rest with my own eyes, not yours."

I do not trouble myself with which store worries me most - the grain is deep, the fish and meat run thin come winter, that is the way of things every year, spirit or no. If you have watched us so long, tell me something I could not know myself - when the first frost comes, or where the fish run thick this year. Words of rain in summer are easy words; any old woman by the fire says as much. Prove your sight to me, and I will listen closer next planting.
